topic: Agentic AI: Orchestrating Enterprise AI Operations

slides.hook: Your AI pilot is a cul‑de‑sac

slides.title: Pilots work. Production stalls.
slides.body: Teams can build clever agent demos, but they die in the handover to operations—no owner, no SLA, no budget line, no integration into how work actually gets done.

slides.title: You shipped tech, not an operation
slides.body: Agentic AI only pays off when it is treated like a business capability—with roles, runbooks, risk controls and KPIs—not as a one‑off innovation artefact.

slides.title: Governance arrives after the damage
slides.body: Most firms bolt on AI governance once agents are live. By then, shadow use, data leakage and inconsistent decisions are already embedded into core workflows.

slides.title: Your people don’t trust the agents
slides.body: Without clear guardrails, escalation paths and training, staff either bypass the system or over‑rely on it—both quietly erode service quality and accountability.

slides.title: No operating model, no scale
slides.body: If every new agent is a bespoke project, you cannot scale. You need a repeatable way to design, approve, deploy and monitor agents across functions.

slides.title: Oversight is manual and reactive
slides.body: Tickets only surface when something breaks. Mature setups treat agents like digital colleagues—continuous monitoring, performance reviews and retraining cycles.

slides.title: Vendors own the critical knowledge
slides.body: When external partners build everything, your teams never learn to tune, govern or extend the agents. Dependency risk climbs just as usage becomes business‑critical.

caption:
Your AI pilot is not an AI operation.

Agentic AI can choreograph complex work across your organisation—but only if you treat it as an operating capability, not a lab experiment.
Most enterprises stall between “great demo” and “reliable system”: no owner, no guardrails, no training, no way to scale beyond a few fragile use cases.
